name: PyTorch
title: What Actually Happens When You Run a PyTorch Model? | Language Lineage
h1: What Actually Happens When You Run a PyTorch Model?
description: Trace a PyTorch model from Python to the hardware: eager vs torch.compile on a CPU, NVIDIA, AMD (ROCm) or Apple (MPS) GPU, through ATen, TorchInductor and Triton, with sources.
og_subtitle: Python → ATen or TorchDynamo → TorchInductor → Triton → CPU · NVIDIA · AMD · Apple GPU
verified_against: PyTorch 2.15 documentation, Triton main README, NVIDIA PTX ISA documentation, the PyTorch MPS backend and HIP (ROCm) semantics notes, TorchInductor's MPS code generator source, and the Triton README
scope: Illustrative, documented paths for one PyTorch program in eager mode and under torch.compile with the default TorchInductor backend, on a CPU, an NVIDIA GPU, an AMD GPU with ROCm, or an Apple silicon GPU (mps). Not every PyTorch program takes these paths: other torch.compile backends, Intel GPUs, CUDA graphs, custom operators and the CPU fallback for operators MPS does not implement are out of scope.
answer: In **eager mode**, each tensor operation in your Python code is a separate call into ATen, PyTorch's C++ core, which runs a precompiled C++ kernel on the CPU or a CUDA kernel on the GPU. With **torch.compile**, TorchDynamo captures runs of operations as an FX graph, and TorchInductor generates new kernels for it: C++ with OpenMP for CPUs, Triton for GPUs. On an NVIDIA GPU, Triton lowers each kernel through MLIR and LLVM IR to PTX, which NVIDIA's driver turns into the GPU's own machine code. On an **AMD GPU**, the ROCm build reuses the torch.cuda interface over HIP, and Triton emits AMDGCN instead of PTX. On an **Apple silicon GPU** (the **mps** device), eager operations run as Metal Performance Shaders graphs and kernels; torch.compile there is an early prototype that turns elementwise operations into Metal shaders.

sections.heading: Where Python ends
paragraphs: In eager mode, Python's part ends at each operation's call into ATen: from there on, everything is precompiled C++ and CUDA that shipped inside PyTorch. Python is still in charge of the order of operations, one call at a time, so the interpreter's overhead is paid on every operation.

Under torch.compile, Python's part ends earlier for the code TorchDynamo can capture: the captured operations never run as individual Python calls again. They become an FX graph, then new code generated by TorchInductor, and on a GPU that code passes through three compiler stages (Triton, LLVM, PTX) before NVIDIA's driver produces machine code for the specific GPU. Code Dynamo cannot trace causes a graph break and still runs in normal Python between compiled graphs.
Either way the GPU work is asynchronous: Python queues kernels and moves on, which is why a GPU program can look fast until something forces it to wait for a result.

sections.heading: AMD and Apple GPUs
paragraphs: PyTorch's ROCm build keeps the CUDA-facing interface: you still write **device='cuda'**, and the calls land on HIP kernels and AMD libraries. Under torch.compile, TorchInductor uses the same Triton route as on NVIDIA GPUs, and Triton emits AMD machine code instead of PTX.

On a Mac, the **mps** device sends operations to Apple's Metal Performance Shaders. torch.compile's MPS support is much younger: its code generator describes itself as an early prototype for elementwise operations. For a framework built for Apple silicon from the start, see [how MLX runs](/ai/how-mlx-runs).

out_of_scope_note: Library routing on AMD (hipBLAS for matrix multiplies, AOTriton for attention) is the documented default; other ROCm backends can be selected. TorchInductor's MPS backend is described by its own source as an early prototype for elementwise operations, so most operations on Apple GPUs still run as MPS kernels. Other torch.compile backends replace TorchInductor entirely.

inductor_design.title: TorchInductor design post by its lead author (PyTorch dev-discuss)

stages.name: Your model code
stages.summary: The nn.Module and training or inference loop you write in Python. Every tensor operation in it is a call into PyTorch.

evidence.quote: ATen is fundamentally a tensor library, on top of which almost all other Python and C++ interfaces in PyTorch are built.

stages.name: CPython interpreter
stages.summary: Runs your Python bytecode. In eager mode it calls PyTorch one operation at a time; under torch.compile, TorchDynamo hooks into it before each frame runs.

evidence.quote: Dynamo hooks into the frame evaluation API in CPython (PEP 523) to dynamically modify Python bytecode right before it is executed.

stages.name: ATen dispatch
stages.summary: PyTorch's C++ tensor library. Each operation is looked up and sent to the implementation for the tensor's device and type.

evidence.quote: Most of these operations have both CPU and GPU implementations, to which the Tensor class will dynamically dispatch based on its type.

stages.name: ATen CPU kernels
stages.summary: Precompiled C++ implementations of each operation for the CPU, shipped inside the PyTorch library.

evidence.quote: Most of these operations have both CPU and GPU implementations, to which the Tensor class will dynamically dispatch based on its type.

stages.name: ATen CUDA kernels
stages.summary: Precompiled GPU implementations of each operation. Some, such as matrix multiplications, call NVIDIA's cuBLAS library.

evidence.quote: Most of these operations have both CPU and GPU implementations, to which the Tensor class will dynamically dispatch based on its type.
Under torch.compile, FP32 matmuls using bfx9 remain ATen/cuBLAS calls

stages.name: TorchDynamo
stages.summary: A Python-level JIT compiler. It rewrites your function's bytecode so that runs of PyTorch operations are captured as a graph instead of executed one by one.

evidence.quote: It rewrites Python bytecode to extract sequences of PyTorch operations into an FX Graph which is then compiled with a customizable backend.

stages.name: FX graph
stages.summary: The captured sequence of PyTorch operations, as a graph a backend compiler can optimize. Code Dynamo cannot trace causes a graph break and runs in normal Python between graphs.

evidence.quote: It rewrites Python bytecode to extract sequences of PyTorch operations into an FX Graph which is then compiled with a customizable backend.
Dynamo performs a graph break when it encounters code that can't be traced.

stages.name: TorchInductor
stages.summary: The default torch.compile backend. It generates new kernels for the graph: Triton for GPUs and C++ for CPUs. For training, AOT Autograd also captures the backward pass ahead of time.

evidence.quote: The default backend is called TorchInductor
TorchInductor is the default compiler backend for TorchDynamo, which translates PyTorch programs into OpenAI's Triton for GPUs and C++ for CPUs.
AOT Autograd captures not only the user-level code, but also backpropagation
Pointwise ops can be fused with: other pointwise ops; reduction ops; and matmul/conv templates.

stages.name: C++/OpenMP kernels
stages.summary: On CPU, Inductor writes C++ kernels that use OpenMP to spread work across cores, usually fusing several operations into one kernel.

evidence.quote: TorchInductor is the default compiler backend for TorchDynamo, which translates PyTorch programs into OpenAI's Triton for GPUs and C++ for CPUs.
OpenMP provides a work sharing parallel execution model, and enables support for CPUs.

stages.name: Triton kernels
stages.summary: On GPU, Inductor writes kernels in Triton, a Python-embedded language for GPU programming, usually fusing several operations into one kernel.

evidence.quote: For NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs, it leverages OpenAI Triton as the key building block.
Triton is a language and compiler for parallel programming.

stages.name: Triton compiler
stages.summary: Compiles each Triton kernel through a series of MLIR passes, then hands it to LLVM for code generation.

evidence.quote: Triton is a language and compiler for parallel programming.
MLIR_ENABLE_DUMP=1 dumps the IR before every MLIR pass Triton runs, for all kernels.

stages.name: LLVM IR
stages.summary: LLVM's intermediate representation. Triton uses LLVM to generate the device code.

evidence.quote: Triton uses LLVM to generate code for GPUs and CPUs.

stages.name: PTX
stages.summary: NVIDIA's virtual instruction set, the last portable step. It is not yet the GPU's own machine code.

evidence.quote: TRITON_KERNEL_DUMP enables the dumping of the IR from each compilation stage and the final ptx/amdgcn.
PTX defines a virtual machine and ISA for general purpose parallel thread execution.

stages.name: GPU machine code
stages.summary: The instructions of one specific GPU architecture, produced from PTX by NVIDIA's translator and driver.

evidence.quote: The PTX-to-GPU translator and driver enable NVIDIA GPUs to be used as programmable parallel computers.

stages.name: CPU
stages.summary: Runs the compiled C++ kernels directly, across its cores.

evidence.quote: OpenMP provides a work sharing parallel execution model, and enables support for CPUs.

stages.name: NVIDIA GPU
stages.summary: Runs kernels launched from the CPU. Launches are queued, so Python usually returns before the GPU has finished.

evidence.quote: By default, GPU operations are asynchronous. When you call a function that uses the GPU, the operations are enqueued to the particular device, but not necessarily executed until later.

stages.name: ATen HIP kernels
stages.summary: On a ROCm build, ATen's GPU kernels are HIP code behind the same torch.cuda interface; by default, matrix multiplies go to hipBLAS and attention to AOTriton.

evidence.quote: PyTorch for HIP intentionally reuses the existing torch.cuda interfaces.
HIP is ROCm’s C++ dialect designed to ease conversion of CUDA applications to portable C++ code.
For GEMMs, this will route to hipblas and for SDPA it routes to aotriton.

stages.name: MPS Graph and kernels
stages.summary: On the mps device, ATen maps operations onto Apple's Metal Performance Shaders Graph framework and the tuned kernels of Metal Performance Shaders.

evidence.quote: It introduces a new device to map Machine Learning computational graphs and primitives on highly efficient Metal Performance Shaders Graph framework and tuned kernels provided by Metal Performance Shaders framework respectively.

stages.name: Metal shaders
stages.summary: TorchInductor's MPS backend, an early prototype, compiles elementwise operations into Metal shaders.

evidence.quote: Just an early prototype that shows that one can compile elementwise ops into a Metal shader

stages.name: AMDGCN
stages.summary: AMD GPU machine code, the final output of Triton's compilation for AMD GPUs (where PTX is the output for NVIDIA).

evidence.quote: enables the dumping of the IR from each compilation stage and the final ptx/amdgcn

stages.name: AMD GPU
stages.summary: An AMD GPU with ROCm, used through the torch.cuda interface.

evidence.quote: PyTorch for HIP intentionally reuses the existing torch.cuda interfaces.

stages.name: Apple silicon GPU
stages.summary: The GPU of an Apple silicon Mac, used through the mps device.

evidence.quote: It introduces a new device to map Machine Learning computational graphs and primitives on highly efficient Metal Performance Shaders Graph framework and tuned kernels provided by Metal Performance Shaders framework respectively.
